procedural_history.originating_court: VI Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Bengaluru (Trial Magistrate)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 18.02.2021, passed by the High Court of Karnataka, at Bengaluru, dismissing Criminal Revision Petition No. 692 / 2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellants initially sought quashing of the chargesheet via Criminal Petition No. 3600 / 2012 in the High Court under Section 482 of the CrPC, which was dismissed on 22.04.2014. The High Court granted liberty to approach the Trial Magistrate to seek discharge. After the Trial Magistrate denied discharge, the Appellants filed Criminal Revision Petition No. 692 / 2018 in the High Court challenging the Trial Magistrate’s order, but the High Court dismissed it on 18.02.2021, primarily because there were specific allegations against the Appellants which required a full-fledged trial.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants, aggrieved by the High Court's judgment dated 18.02.2021, approached the Supreme Court by filing Criminal Appeal No. 335 of 2024.

directions: The impugned judgment of the High Court dated 18.02.2021 is set aside.
The order of the Trial Magistrate dated 15.03.2018 is set aside.

FIR No. 141 / 2010 registered at Police Station Adugodi, Bengaluru under Sections 420, 468, 471 read with Section 34 IPC, lodged by Respondent No. 2 against the Appellants and all the proceedings arising therefrom are quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a prima facie case, to subject the Appellants to the agony of trial, has been made out.

facts: The Appellants were charged with offenses including cheating (Section 420 IPC) and forgery (Sections 468, 471 IPC).
The Trial Magistrate found sufficient grounds to frame charges and declined to discharge the Appellants.
The High Court upheld the Trial Magistrate's decision, stating that the allegations required a full-fledged trial.
The aggrieved Appellants then appealed to the Supreme Court.
law: The Supreme Court examined whether the elementary ingredients of 'cheating' and 'forgery' were prima facie established against the Appellants at the very threshold.
For cheating, the Court looked for evidence of deception, dishonest inducement for the delivery of property, and resulting damage.
For forgery, the Court considered the elements required under Sections 468 and 471 IPC.
application: The Court analyzed the facts and allegations presented in the case.
It found that the Trial Magistrate had failed to approach the complaint with "due care and circumspection" and had not made even a "cursory effort to discern the actual ‘victim’ or ‘victimiser’".
Upon its own review, the Supreme Court determined that the "elementary ingredients of ‘cheating’ and ‘forgery’ are conspicuously missing" from the case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that no prima facie case was made out against the Appellants. It held that continuing the criminal proceedings would be an "abuse of the process of law" and therefore rejected the lower courts' findings.

issue.issue_text: Whether there has been a prima facie case made out for forgery under Sections 468 and 471 IPC?

facts: The central allegation against the appellants was that they had forged the signature of respondent No. 2 on a passport application for a minor child.
law: The Court outlined the two essential components required to establish the offence of 'forgery' under Section 468 IPC: (i) the accused must have fabricated a false document, and (ii) this must be done with the dishonest intention that the forged document would be used for the purpose of cheating, which implies an intent to cause damage or injury.
Section 471 IPC punishes anyone who fraudulently or dishonestly uses a document they know to be forged as if it were genuine.
application: The Court analyzed the facts of the case against the legal requirements for forgery. It noted that the core of the offence is not merely the creation of a false document, but the specific intent behind its creation.

To make out a prima facie case, the prosecution had to show not only that the signature was fabricated, but also that it was done with a dishonest intention to cause damage or injury for the purpose of cheating.
The Court found that this crucial element of dishonest intent was not established from the material gathered by the investigating agency.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a prima facie case for forgery under Sections 468 and 471 of the IPC was not made out against the appellants because the essential ingredient of a dishonest intention to cause damage or injury for the purpose of cheating was not established.

issue.issue_text: Whether there has been a violation of Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, 1967?

facts: The appellants were accused of forging the signature of Respondent No. 2 on a passport application for a minor child.
A State Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) report concluded that the alleged forgery of the signature on the passport application was 'inconclusive'.
No complaint regarding this offense was filed by the 'Prescribed Authority' (the relevant passport authority).
law: Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, 1967, makes it an offense to 'knowingly furnish any false information or suppress any material information' with the intent to obtain a passport.
For a court to take cognizance of an offense under this section, a complaint must be initiated by the 'Prescribed Authority'.
application: The Court determined that the 'inconclusive' FSL report failed to establish the core requirement of the offense: that the appellants had 'knowingly furnished false information'.
The Court also identified a critical procedural failure: the absence of a complaint from the Prescribed Authority, which is a legal prerequisite for prosecuting such an offense.
The Court reasoned that it could not proceed on 'conjectures and surmises' in the absence of conclusive evidence and proper procedure.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim of a violation of Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, 1967, for two main reasons: first, the evidence of forgery was inconclusive, and second, the legally required complaint from the Prescribed Authority was never filed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Trial Magistrate was correct in allowing the prayer for further investigation under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. and proceeding with the case.

facts: Respondent No. 2 requested a 'further investigation' under Section 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
The Trial Magistrate granted this request on 24.06.2015.
Following this, the investigating agency filed a supplementary charge-sheet.
This supplementary charge-sheet did not contain any new material or evidence unearthed during the 'further investigation'.
Instead, it relied on a 'Truth Lab report' that was already available when the original charge-sheet was filed.
law: Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. defines 'further investigation' as the process of obtaining 'further evidence, oral or documentary'.

This provision requires that fresh evidence be obtained, rather than simply re-evaluating or reassessing material that was already collected and considered for the initial police report (charge-sheet).
application: The Supreme Court found that the investigation conducted after the Magistrate's order did not meet the legal standard of a 'further investigation' under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C.
Since no new evidence was discovered and the supplementary report was based on a pre-existing document, the process was merely a re-evaluation of old material.
The Court concluded that the investigating agency had acted mechanically and the resulting supplementary report lacked the necessary 'investigative rigour'.
A report that fails to present new evidence does not satisfy the requirements of the law, and a Magistrate is not compelled to take cognizance of it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the Trial Magistrate's decision, holding that it was incorrect to allow the prayer for further investigation because the subsequent investigation and supplementary report failed to comply with the legal requirements of Section 173(8) Cr.P.C., as no new evidence was actually obtained.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a prima facie case, to subject the Appellants to the agony of trial, has been made out.
appellant_arguments: There were no grounds to frame charges against them.
respondent_arguments: There were specific allegations against the Appellants which required a full-fledged trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there has been a prima facie case made out for forgery under Sections 468 and 471 IPC?
appellant_arguments: There were no grounds to frame charges for forgery, as they did not forge the respondent's signatures.
respondent_arguments: The Appellants had forged the respondent's signatures on the minor child’s passport application and submitted it to the Regional Passport Office.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there has been a violation of Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, 1967?
appellant_arguments: The appellants' actions regarding the passport application did not constitute a violation of the Passports Act.
respondent_arguments: The act of submitting a passport application with allegedly forged signatures constitutes a violation of the Passports Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Trial Magistrate was correct in allowing the prayer for further investigation under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. and proceeding with the case.
appellant_arguments: The Trial Magistrate was incorrect to proceed with the case and frame charges based on the supplementary charge-sheet that resulted from the further investigation.
respondent_arguments: The Trial Magistrate was correct to allow further investigation and proceed with the case based on the findings in the supplementary charge-sheet.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, the appellant-wife seems to have breached the notion of mutual marital trust and unauthorizedly projected respondent no. 2’s consent in obtaining the passport for their minor child – It, however, remains a question as to how such an act can be labelled as ‘deceitful’ – The motivations prompting either of the appellants to procure a passport for the minor child were not rooted in deceit – Furthermore, the grant of passport to the minor child did not confer any benefit upon the appellan-wife, nor did it result in any loss or damage to respondent no. 2.
legal_tests_applied: For an offence of cheating, it must be prima facie established that: (i) the Appellants have deceived Respondent No. 2; (ii) Respondent No. 2 was induced with dishonest intentions; (iii) such inducement was for the delivery of any property or valuable security; and (iv) as a result of such an act, Respondent No. 2 has suffered some damage or injury.

For an offence under Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, it must be established that the accused knowingly furnished false information or suppressed material information with the intent of obtaining a passport or travel document.
For an offence under the Passports Act, cognizance can be taken only at the instance of the Prescribed Authority.
policy_considerations: The right to travel abroad is a fundamental right of an individual, albeit not absolute, and subject to established legal procedures.

The conduct exhibited by Respondent No. 2 infringes upon the best interests of the minor child, which necessitates the child’s travel abroad for the realisation of opportunities and intrinsic value, aligning with the child’s dignity, as enshrined by the Constitution.
This Court, therefore, will exercise caution before invoking such severe offences and penalties solely on the basis of conjectures and surmises.
